The experiments are described as real-world and extensive, but the abstract does not specify datasets, languages, platforms, adversarial behavior, or how the system behaves when users deliberately change tactics after detection begins.

98.bp: The ordinary object in this paper is not a new security invention. It is the visible surface of everyday Internet service: domain names, web servers, name lookup, mail-related records, transport settings, and other public signals that tell whether a service has installed basic protections. People rely on those services for confidentiality, integrity, and availability: keeping private communication private, keeping records from being changed unnoticed, and keeping services reachable. The paper matters because the Internet can advertise new waves such as Web3 and artificial intelligence while still leaving old doors unlocked. A country-level operator, regulator, researcher, or domain owner needs a sober map of these basics before deciding where resilience is actually weak. The paper therefore asks a measurement question: among known German .de domains, which foundational security measures are present, absent, or unevenly deployed? Katti is the tool used for that measurement, but the deeper purpose is to turn scattered security hygiene into a systematic picture.
98.wh: The hard part is that Internet security is spread across many layers and many independent owners. One domain may have a web server, another may only hold a parked name, another may run mail, and each layer has its own mature protective measures. A simple yes-or-no label such as secure domain would hide this unevenness. The abstract says the results show substantial heterogeneity across indicators, which means different protections are deployed at different rates. Measurement also has to avoid becoming an attack. If a study probes too aggressively, it can disturb services, trigger alarms, or require permission from every operator. If it relies on voluntary surveys, the view will be incomplete and biased toward organizations willing to answer. The central tension is therefore breadth versus restraint: the study wants population-level coverage of known .de domains while checking only indicators that are standardized, mature, and visible from outside without intrusive behavior.
98.naive: A smart beginner might ask every domain owner to fill out a security checklist, then count the answers. That fails because many owners will not respond, some will misunderstand their own setup, and the least prepared operators may be least likely to participate. Another beginner move is to inspect a few famous websites and treat them as a proxy for the whole national domain space. That fails because large, professionally managed services are not representative of small businesses, parked domains, hobby sites, or neglected records. A third move is to run deep vulnerability scans. That may find richer detail, but it changes the ethical and operational problem: intrusive scans can look like attacks and may not be acceptable at the scale of all known .de domains.
98.ap: The core idea is to define a baseline security indicator as a public, mature, standardized sign that a foundational protection has been deployed. Instead of asking whether a domain is generally safe, the paper breaks safety into checkable pieces across the Internet stack. Each piece acts like a light on a control panel: not a full guarantee, but a concrete signal that one basic practice is present. Because the indicators can be analyzed non-intrusively, Katti can examine a very large population without needing private logs, passwords, cooperation from site owners, or active exploitation. The move is deliberately conservative. The study is not chasing the newest attack or the most advanced defense. It asks whether the basic defenses that are already well known have actually reached deployed services. That turns security from a story about innovation into a measurable deployment problem.
98.mech: The mechanism starts with a population: the known .de domains in the German Internet landscape. For each domain, Katti checks a set of baseline security indicators. The abstract does not list the individual indicators, so the safe reading is general: each indicator corresponds to a foundational measure at some layer of the Internet stack and must be widely standardized, operationally mature, and externally observable. The input is therefore a domain plus public protocol behavior or public configuration data. Katti transforms that input into indicator observations: present, absent, reachable, supported, or otherwise measurable according to the rule for that indicator. The system then aggregates those observations across the domain population. One output is a per-indicator deployment view: how common each measure is. Another output is a cross-indicator comparison: whether adoption is consistent or uneven. This matters because a domain can do well on one layer and poorly on another, and the national picture can contain pockets of strength and weakness at the same time. The final product is not a certificate that any single domain is perfectly secure. It is a systematic overview of foundational security deployment, built from externally visible evidence rather than self-report. The preliminary findings then identify the practical gap named in the abstract: a significant fraction of domains still fail to implement basic measures.
98.math: The main mathematical idea is measurement by indicators. An indicator is a deliberately simplified observable sign: it does not contain the whole truth, but it answers one narrow question reliably enough to count. This paper uses indicators because Internet security is too broad to measure directly as one object. The method turns a messy technical landscape into a table where rows are domains and columns are basic protections. Counting then becomes meaningful: for each column, the study can estimate deployment across the known .de population. Comparison is the second idea. If two indicators have very different deployment levels, the difference reveals where operational adoption is uneven, not just whether security exists in the abstract. The information concept is also central. A public check is useful when it rules out uncertainty about one practice without exposing private internals. The tradeoff is detail versus coverage: narrow indicators miss many subtle risks, but because they are standardized and non-intrusive, they can be applied broadly. The network and systems view matters too. A domain is a node in a larger Internet landscape, and weak baseline deployment across many nodes affects collective resilience. The math is not complicated for its own sake; it is disciplined counting under constraints, where the constraint is to learn useful security facts without crossing operational or privacy boundaries.
98.dots: This paper connects to the repo's privacy, federated, and security family through the shared question of what evidence can safely cross a boundary. Many papers in that family ask how to learn, verify, or audit without exposing private records. This one asks a simpler but related question: what can be learned about security posture from public signals alone? It also connects to information-centered papers because each indicator is a small uncertainty-reducing message. Seeing that a domain lacks a basic measure does not explain the owner's intent, but it changes what we know about exposure. It connects to network reasoning because the result is population-level: resilience is not only the strength of a few major services but the pattern of adoption across many domains. It also sits beside Web3 and artificial-intelligence security work as a warning that new paradigms do not erase old operational duties. The conference-level theme is security as measurement, not only security as new defense design.
98.ww: The approach works better than the naive survey or spot-check because it chooses evidence that is both comparable and broadly collectible. A self-report mixes technical reality with memory, incentives, and misunderstanding. A few manual inspections mix real detail with selection bias. A deep scan may find more, but it cannot easily justify itself across an entire national domain population. Baseline indicators avoid those traps by asking questions that services already answer through normal public behavior or public configuration. Because the indicators are standardized and mature, absence is meaningful: if a foundational measure is missing, the paper can reasonably treat that as a deployment gap rather than as failure to adopt an experimental idea. Because the same checks are applied across known .de domains, heterogeneity becomes visible. The study can show that some protections have diffused while others remain neglected. That is the causal intuition behind the measurement: repeated, uniform, low-intrusion checks turn many small public observations into a map of where basic resilience has and has not become routine.
98.po: The payoff is a grounded view of Internet security hygiene across the German .de landscape. The abstract says the preliminary results provide a systematic overview and reveal substantial heterogeneity across indicators, with a significant fraction of domains failing to implement foundational measures. That gives operators and policymakers a practical target: not merely inventing newer defenses, but increasing adoption of mature ones. It also gives researchers a baseline for future comparison. If the same indicators are measured again, progress or stagnation can be tracked. The capability bought is large-scale situational awareness about basic security deployment, produced without requiring intrusive access to services.
98.limits: The abstract leaves important boundaries. It does not list the exact indicators, the measurement rules, the date of observation, or how Katti handles unreachable, parked, duplicate, or unusual domains. Baseline indicators are only signs of deployed measures; they do not prove correct configuration, absence of vulnerabilities, good incident response, or real protection against all attacks. The case study covers known .de domains, so the findings should not automatically be generalized to all countries or all Internet services. The results are described as preliminary. The approach also assumes that public, non-intrusive observations accurately reflect deployment and that the chosen mature indicators capture the most important basics for long-term resilience.

99.bp: Online deception often works by making two ordinary channels support each other. A picture gives the feeling of direct evidence, while a caption or article tells the reader what the picture supposedly means. The hard case is not only a fake picture or a false sentence. It can be a true picture used with a false caption, a true sentence placed beside the wrong picture, or two individually true pieces arranged so their pairing suggests a false event. This paper serves the systems that must sort such posts before they travel through feeds, search results, chats, or news pages. Its starting point is that multimodal disinformation has more structure than a simple true-or-false label. The authors separate three questions: whether the image is truthful, whether the text is truthful, and whether the two fit each other. That creates an eight-part map of possible cases, giving detectors and datasets a clearer target.
99.wh: The difficulty is that a mixed image-text post can be wrong in several different places, and those places do not fail in the same way. If the image is fabricated, the detector needs evidence about visual authenticity. If the text makes a false factual claim, the detector needs evidence about language and real-world truth. If both are individually truthful but mismatched, the detector needs to notice the relation between them. A coarse label such as fake news hides these differences. A multi-label setup can say several things are wrong, but the abstract argues that prior work has not covered the full range of combinations, so methods trained on familiar cases may be surprised by unseen ones. The central tension is coverage versus clarity: the system must describe every possible mixture, but the categories also need to be clean enough that a model can make one final decision rather than a confused collection of overlapping alarms.
99.naive: A smart beginner would train one large detector on image-text posts and ask it to output real or fake. That looks natural because platforms often need a single moderation decision. It fails because the same final label can come from different mechanisms. A real disaster photo with a false location caption is not the same evidence problem as a generated photo with accurate text about a real issue. The beginner might then make three separate binary labels and leave them independent. That helps, but it can still produce incomplete or overlapping outcomes if the data does not cover every combination. This paper's abstract says existing research has left combinations unconsidered, which means a detector can look competent on known cases while having no well-defined answer for a new mixture.
99.ap: The core move is to turn a vague detection problem into a small, complete checklist. The paper treats every post as having three yes-or-no axes. First, is the image itself truthful? Second, is the text itself truthful? Third, are the image and text consistent with each other? Three binary axes produce eight possible boxes, like eight rooms in a building. Each post should belong to exactly one room, because every image-text pair has one setting on each axis. This is the tri-axis formulation. It changes the task from a coarse, possibly overlapping judgment into an exhaustive classification task, where exhaustive means the map has a place for every combination described by the axes. OctantFake supplies data for all eight rooms by drawing from sixteen datasets. OctantAgent then checks the three axes in parallel and fuses those three judgments into the final eight-way decision.
99.mech: The mechanism begins with one multimodal item: an image and an associated text. The first branch examines the image as its own evidence source and predicts whether the image is truthful or misleading. The second branch examines the text as its own evidence source and predicts whether the written claim is truthful or misleading. The third branch examines the relation between them and predicts whether the words match what the picture supports. These branches are parallel, so the image check does not have to solve text truth, the text check does not have to solve visual authenticity, and the consistency check can focus on the gap between channels. Their outputs are then fused. Fusion here means combining the three yes-or-no judgments into one of the eight possible combinations: image status, text status, and cross-modal status together define the final class. The dataset construction matters because a fusion rule is only useful if the model has seen examples from every room in the taxonomy. OctantFake is built from sixteen datasets with complete label coverage and broad class diversity, so training and evaluation can include all eight cases rather than only the easy or common ones. Experiments then compare existing methods and the proposed large vision-language model based agent system on this harder, better specified task.
99.math: The main mathematical idea is a product of simple choices. A binary choice has two possible values. Three independent axes, each with two values, make two times two times two, or eight, possible states. This is not fancy math, but it is important because it forces completeness. If image truth, text truth, and cross-modal consistency are the three things that can fail, then every post can be located by its position on those three axes. The second idea is mutually exclusive classification: the final answer should be one box, not several boxes at once. That matters because overlapping labels can hide contradictions, while one-of-eight labeling makes the detector say exactly which failure pattern it sees. The third idea is evidence decomposition, or splitting a hard judgment into smaller judgments whose results are recombined. In ordinary terms, instead of asking one person to inspect the photograph, fact-check the sentence, and judge the pairing all at once, the system assigns these as three separate checks. The tradeoff is clarity versus dependency. The axes make the task interpretable, but the checks may not be truly independent in the world: deciding whether text is truthful can depend on what the image shows, and deciding image truth can depend on context from the text.
99.dots: This paper sits at the intersection of misinformation detection and multimodal reasoning in the repo's current map. The misinformation-trust family treats trust as an evidence chain rather than a single label: source, content, context, and final confidence can each break. This paper makes that chain concrete for image-text posts by naming three breakpoints. It also belongs to the multimodal vision-language family, where the recurring problem is that text and images can each be useful alone, but the hardest cases live in their relation. Neighboring papers in the project check retrieved evidence for fact verification, inspect video fake news with outside references, study AI-generated disinformation, or analyze out-of-context media. The shared deeper problem is controlled comparison under uncertainty: decide which evidence source is speaking, whether it should be trusted, and whether two sources really support the same claim. OctantFake contributes a taxonomy and dataset foundation, while OctantAgent is one concrete detector built on that foundation.
99.ww: The approach should work better than the naive one because it matches the shape of the failure. When a detector only predicts fake or real, it must compress many different reasons into one answer. That compression can erase the clue needed for the next case. A model that has mainly seen false captions on real images may not handle a false image paired with true text, because the visible pattern of deception is different. The eight-way map prevents that blind spot by requiring complete coverage of the combinations described in the abstract. The parallel checks also give each module a narrower job. The image branch can look for whether the visual evidence itself is trustworthy, the text branch can assess the written claim, and the consistency branch can ask whether the two tell the same story. Combining those judgments gives a more diagnostic answer: not just that something is wrong, but where the wrongness appears. The abstract's experimental claim fits this logic: existing methods struggle on the more challenging OctantFake dataset, while the modular large vision-language model based agent improves over existing methods of that kind.
99.po: The payoff is a clearer foundation for analyzing multimodal disinformation. Instead of treating a post as merely true or false, the system can say whether the problem lies in the image, the text, the pairing, or some combination of those. OctantFake gives researchers an eight-way dataset with complete label coverage and class diversity from sixteen sources, so they can test detectors against cases that older work may have missed. OctantAgent shows that a detector organized around the three checks can improve over existing large vision-language model based methods. For platforms or fact-checking tools, the useful capability is a more interpretable warning about what kind of deception is present.
99.limits: The claims depend on the tri-axis formulation being the right map for the domain. It covers image truth, text truth, and image-text consistency, but the abstract does not prove that every socially important form of disinformation fits cleanly into those axes. The dataset is sourced from sixteen datasets, so its coverage still depends on their labeling quality, cultures, topics, and media styles. The parallel modules also depend on the large vision-language model's ability to judge image, text, and consistency reliably. The abstract reports clear improvements, but it does not establish long-term performance against coordinated adversaries, new media formats, sarcasm, missing context, or rapidly changing events.

100.bp: A review sentence often contains more than one opinion. A restaurant review may praise the service and complain about the food; a phone review may like the camera and dislike the battery. The practical task here is to decide the sentiment polarity for one specified aspect, not for the whole sentence. That matters anywhere organizations read large volumes of feedback and need to know which part of a product, service, or issue people like or dislike. The paper focuses on a common failure in this setting: a learned text model can appear accurate while relying on surface patterns that travel with labels in the training data. It may notice words, positions, or repeated phrasing that usually accompany positive or negative labels, while missing the aspect-related clue that should actually decide the answer. CECR is proposed to make the model reason as if the aspect-specific evidence, rather than accidental wording, is the driver of the sentiment judgment.
100.wh: The hard part is that ordinary sentences mix target evidence with distracting evidence. The specified aspect is only one object inside the sentence, and surrounding words may describe another object, set up a contrast, or carry a general tone that does not belong to the target aspect. A deep model trained only to match sentences to labels can exploit whatever shortcut reduces past mistakes. If a surface pattern often appears with a label, the model may treat that pattern as a rule even when the real reason is different. This is what the abstract calls spurious correlation: two things appear together in the data, but one is not the true reason for the other. The model then becomes fragile. It may work on familiar datasets yet fail when phrasing changes, when the same sentiment word points to a different aspect, or when a sentence contains several opinions. The central tension is between correlation that is easy to learn and aspect-related evidence that is harder but more trustworthy.
100.naive: A smart beginner would feed the sentence and target aspect into a sentiment classifier and let the model learn from labeled examples. The model would see many cases where an aspect is marked positive, negative, or neutral, then learn word patterns that predict those labels. That can work when the training examples cover the same style as future examples. It fails because the easiest predictive clue is not always the right clue. The word that looks emotional may refer to another aspect. A frequent phrase may reflect dataset habits rather than meaning. A model trained this way is rewarded for being right on old cases, not for knowing which words would still matter if the irrelevant parts of the sentence were changed.
100.ap: The paper's central move is to create and use alternate versions of training examples so the model cannot survive on accidental shortcuts alone. At the data level, CECR includes a counterfactual data augmentation module. Counterfactual means an imagined near-copy of an example where a meaningful part is changed so the system can ask what the label should become. The abstract says this generation follows a three-stage reasoning process guided by chain-of-thought principles, meaning the system is pushed to construct these alternate examples through explicit intermediate reasoning rather than a single unexamined rewrite. At the model level, CECR adds multi-level causal attention. Attention here means assigning different influence to different words or features before making the prediction. The causal version is intended to repeatedly pull out features tied to the target aspect and reduce the influence of confounding features, which are distracting factors that explain labels in the dataset without being the true aspect evidence.
100.mech: The mechanism has two cooperating parts. First comes the data side. The input is the original training collection for aspect-based sentiment analysis: sentences, specified aspects, and sentiment labels. The counterfactual data augmentation module takes these examples and generates altered examples. The abstract does not give the exact three stages, so the safe inference is functional: the stages guide the system to identify what should be changed, produce a plausible alternate sentence, and keep the new example high quality enough for training. The purpose is controlled comparison. The original and the alternate example should be similar enough that irrelevant surface habits cannot explain both labels, while the aspect-related evidence is changed or clarified. Second comes the model side. The multi-level causal attention component reads the sentence and aspect, then iteratively separates useful aspect-linked features from confounding features. Iteratively matters because one pass may still mix the target clue with surrounding tone or dataset shortcuts. At each level, the model adjusts which parts of the representation receive influence, keeping signals that better support the specified aspect's sentiment and suppressing signals that look predictive only because they often co-occurred with a label. The final output is the polarity for the specified aspect. Training on original plus counterfactual examples gives the model more direct pressure to base that output on the evidence that should change the answer.
100.math: The main mathematical idea is controlled comparison for cause. Instead of asking only, "Which words often appear with this label?", the paper asks a stronger question: "If the relevant aspect evidence changed while much of the sentence stayed comparable, should the sentiment label change?" That is causal reasoning in plain terms. It tries to separate a driver from a passenger. Counterfactual augmentation supplies paired or near-paired cases, so learning is not based only on raw frequency. The model sees examples designed to expose whether a clue remains valid when the surrounding surface pattern is no longer reliable. The second idea is weighted combining. Multi-level causal attention breaks the sentence representation into parts and gives them unequal influence. These weights are not truth by themselves; they are learned knobs that decide which pieces speak loudly in the final polarity decision. The multi-level design suggests repeated filtering: extract candidate causal features, then reduce the pull of confounding features. The underlying tradeoff is focus versus missing context. Strong focus can protect the model from shortcuts, but if the generated counterfactuals or learned weights are wrong, useful context can be suppressed. The math fits because aspect sentiment is a small decision inside a noisy sentence, where the true evidence is local, mixed with other opinions, and easy to confuse with correlations.
100.dots: This paper connects directly to the repo's cause concept: it tries to stop trusting what appears together and instead ask which controlled change explains the sentiment label. Its closest conference neighbors are other causal papers that repair broken comparisons, such as recommendation work that separates popularity from personal preference, RAG work that treats source conflict as evidence about answer reliability, and security or fault-tracing work that asks which earlier event actually produced a later failure. It also belongs in the text-mining and natural-language family because it turns messy language into a decision under uncertainty. The shared problem in that family is that visible words are not the same as usable evidence. Some text papers solve this with retrieval, some with finer units, some with domain-specific tests. CECR solves the language-evidence mismatch by adding counterfactual examples and selective influence. It also touches the attention concept, not as a fashionable label, but as the practical act of deciding which parts of a sentence should count more for the current aspect.
100.ww: CECR should work better than the naive classifier because it changes what mistakes are expensive during learning. If training only contains ordinary examples, a shortcut can look profitable: the model can reduce errors by relying on a phrase, position, or common co-occurrence that happens to line up with the label. Counterfactual examples make that shortcut less stable. When a near-copy of an example changes the aspect-related evidence, the model is pushed to notice the feature that explains the changed label rather than the background that stayed similar. The multi-level causal attention then applies the same idea inside the model. It does not merely average all sentence information. It gives more influence to features that look tied to the specified aspect and repeatedly reduces features that behave like confounders. This is useful because aspect sentiment is often decided by a small relation: this opinion word describes this aspect, not another one. The reported experimental gains are plausible because the method attacks the failure the abstract names: models that learn surface correlations rather than aspect-related causal features.
100.po: The payoff is a sentiment system that is meant to be less brittle when sentences contain misleading surface patterns. For product reviews, customer feedback, or any setting where one sentence can discuss multiple aspects, this buys a more precise answer: not just whether the sentence sounds positive or negative, but whether the specified aspect carries that polarity. The abstract reports that CECR achieves outstanding performance against strong baselines on the datasets used. More importantly, the capability claimed is improved robustness: the model is trained and structured to depend less on accidental correlations and more on features that should actually explain the aspect-level sentiment.
100.limits: The abstract does not prove that CECR finds true causes in the philosophical or experimental sense. It shows a design intended to reduce spurious correlations through generated counterfactual data and causal attention, then reports dataset results. The method assumes the counterfactual augmentation module can create high-quality alternate examples; poor rewrites could teach new artifacts. It also assumes the attention mechanism can distinguish aspect-related features from confounding features well enough to help. The abstract does not specify datasets, languages, domains, counterfactual quality checks, or behavior under adversarial writing. Its claims are strongest for settings similar to the evaluated ABSA datasets.

101.bp: Large online and technical systems often matter because they stay connected. A web graph lets pages point readers to other pages. A social graph lets claims, rumors, and corrections travel from person to person. An infrastructure graph lets services depend on servers, routers, or other services. Network dismantling asks a deliberately severe planning question: if a harmful spread or a dangerous dependency must be broken, which nodes should be removed so the one huge connected mass is shattered at the lowest cost? The paper is about making that question usable on networks large enough to resemble real systems. The abstract names the Web, system robustness, and misinformation containment because all three depend on the same structure: a giant connected component, meaning one enormous region where many nodes can still reach many others through paths. The work studies how to find removal choices, and how to update them when the network changes.
101.wh: The difficulty is that a network's weak points are not visible from one node alone. A node with many links may look important, but removing it may leave several alternate paths around the damage. A less obvious node may sit between communities, so removing it can separate large regions cheaply. The goal is also minimum cost, not merely maximum damage, so the method must weigh what is removed against how much connectivity is broken. On top of that, real networks change. Pages appear, accounts vanish, links are edited, and infrastructure nodes come and go. If every small change forces a full recomputation, the method is too slow for a 10-million-scale network. The hard part is therefore twofold: choose a small effective removal set in a huge connected object, and keep that choice current without starting over whenever the graph is edited.
101.naive: A smart beginner would sort nodes by an easy importance score, such as number of links, and remove the largest ones first until the giant connected component falls apart. That sounds reasonable because highly connected nodes often help many paths. It fails because link count is local. It cannot see whether neighbors have backup routes, whether a node bridges two big regions, or whether removing several modest nodes together is cheaper than removing one famous hub. Another beginner strategy is to test every possible removal set and keep the cheapest successful one. That fails in the opposite direction: it can be accurate in principle, but the number of possible sets explodes, especially on web-scale graphs.
101.ap: The paper's central move is reverse dismantling. Instead of only asking which nodes to delete from a full network, it looks at the problem from the opposite direction: how would connected structure reappear if nodes were added back in a controlled order? This reversal can reveal which nodes are doing the most work in holding a giant component together. The proposed heuristic, IG+, uses that reverse view plus added efficiency improvements to choose removal candidates without solving the impossible exact search. For changing networks, the paper adds CCRT-ins and CCRT-rem, two dynamic algorithms for insertion and removal cases. They use tree-like indexes, which are stored summaries of connected structure, so the system can update dismantling results after graph changes instead of rebuilding the whole answer from scratch.
101.mech: The input is a graph: nodes stand for pages, people, machines, or other entities, and edges stand for relationships through which connectivity or spread can travel. The target is the giant connected component, the largest region where nodes remain mutually reachable through paths. First, the static method examines the graph through reverse dismantling. Conceptually, it considers the constructive version of the destructive task: as nodes are restored or preserved, which choices most quickly rebuild large connected regions? Nodes that are crucial during this reverse process become strong candidates for removal in the original direction, because their presence helps separated pieces merge. IG+ uses this signal as a fast rule for approximating a low-cost dismantling set. It then applies optimizations described only at a high level in the abstract, so the exact internal scoring details cannot be inferred here. The output is a set or order of nodes whose removal breaks the giant component at the chosen granularity. For dynamic networks, CCRT-ins and CCRT-rem maintain tree-like indexes. When a node or edge is inserted, or when one is removed, the index tells the algorithm which parts of the previous dismantling result may have changed. The method then updates affected structure locally rather than recomputing the full graph answer.
101.math: The main mathematical object is a graph, a map of places and links. Connectivity means reachability: two nodes are connected if some chain of links joins them. A connected component is a whole island of mutually reachable nodes, and the giant connected component is the island so large that it dominates the network. Dismantling is an optimization problem in the plain sense: define what counts as success, define the cost of removing nodes, and search for choices that achieve success with less cost. The reason this is hard is combinatorial growth. With many nodes, the number of possible removal sets becomes far too large to inspect one by one. A heuristic is a disciplined shortcut: it does not promise the perfect answer, but it uses structure in the graph to find a useful answer quickly. Reverse dismantling changes the direction of reasoning, replacing deletion with reconstruction so that bridge-like or merger-causing nodes become easier to spot. The dynamic algorithms add indexing math. A tree-like index stores relationships in a shape where updates can travel through a limited set of branches. The tradeoff is accuracy and freshness versus time and memory: the index costs storage and maintenance, but saves repeated full searches.
101.dots: This paper sits directly in the network family because its object is not a single page, post, or machine, but the shape made by all their links. It connects to misinformation work through containment: if false claims spread along social or web connections, breaking the largest reachable region can limit how far a cascade travels. It connects to system robustness from the opposite angle. Resilience studies often ask which added edges or protections keep a network connected; dismantling asks which removals reveal where the network is fragile. It also connects to efficiency and scalability, because the abstract emphasizes 10-million-scale networks and minute-level running time. Neighboring graph papers in the repo use links to spread evidence for prediction, search, recommendation, or anomaly detection. This paper uses links more adversarially: it asks which connected pieces must be cut so evidence, influence, failure, or traffic can no longer travel through one giant mass.
101.ww: The method should improve over the naive approach because reverse reasoning looks at joint structure rather than isolated node fame. A high-degree node may be replaceable if many alternate paths keep its neighbors connected. A node that causes several separated regions to merge during reconstruction is more informative for dismantling, because deleting it in the original graph can help keep those regions apart. That is the intuitive reason the reverse view fits the task: the same places that rebuild large connectivity are plausible places to remove when the goal is to destroy large connectivity. The dynamic index helps for a different reason. Real graph edits usually affect a limited neighborhood or a limited part of the stored structure. If the algorithm can identify that affected part, it can refresh the dismantling result without paying the cost of reading and scoring the entire network again. This converts a huge repeated task into a sequence of smaller repair tasks. The abstract's effectiveness and efficiency claims are plausible because the method aligns the score with the actual target, the giant component, while avoiding exhaustive search.
101.po: The payoff is a practical dismantling tool for very large networks. The abstract says IG+ outperforms prior approaches in effectiveness and efficiency, and that the methods can dismantle 10-million-scale networks at arbitrary granularity in a few minutes. In practical terms, that means analysts can test how a web graph, social network, or infrastructure network fragments under targeted removals instead of waiting for an offline computation that is too slow to guide decisions. The dynamic algorithms add another capability: when the network changes, the dismantling result can be updated efficiently, which matters for systems that do not stand still.
101.limits: The abstract supports a strong scalability claim, but it does not prove exact optimality. IG+ is described as a heuristic, so its answer should be read as a fast, useful approximation to the minimum-cost removal set, not a guaranteed best set. The method also assumes the graph representation is the right one: nodes and links must capture the paths through which robustness, misinformation, or failure actually travels. If influence moves outside the observed links, dismantling the measured graph may not contain the real process. The dynamic algorithms assume changes can be handled through their tree-like indexes, but the abstract does not specify behavior under massive simultaneous edits, adversarial rewiring, uncertain edge quality, or removal costs that change over time.

102.bp: The ordinary object behind this workshop is a future web full of machines that must prove things to one another: cars, sensors, phones, wallets, edge services, public systems, supply-chain tools, health systems, and AI services. Many of those machines will not sit behind one trusted company account. They will need to connect, authenticate, compute, pay, and audit across organizational boundaries. ZABAPAD treats that as a trust problem before it treats it as a technology problem. Web 2.0 often used IP addresses and platform accounts as anchors. Mobile networks used SIM identity. Web 3.0 used wallets, ledgers, and NFTs. The abstract argues that AIoT and Web 4.0 need a different anchor: verifiable connection where a device or service can prove an allowed fact without exposing the private identity, data, or computation behind it. The workshop's purpose is to organize that transition around zero-knowledge proof systems, blockchains, post-quantum migration, real deployments, measurements, standards, benchmarks, and failure modes.
102.wh: The difficulty is that the desired properties pull against one another. Privacy says do not reveal the secret. Verification says let another party check that the claim is true. Decentralization says do not depend on one central registry or server. Interoperability says many builders, networks, wallets, ledgers, and non-Web systems must still understand one another. Post-quantum readiness adds another pressure: old public-key locks may not remain safe if future quantum computers can solve the problems those locks depend on. AIoT makes the problem messier because devices, vehicles, and edge services are numerous, mobile, and often resource constrained. A proof that is elegant on paper may be too slow, too large, too hard to integrate, or tied to one blockchain stack. A migration plan that protects wallets may ignore mobile identity. A benchmark that works for finance may not expose health-care or mobility failure modes. The hard part is making privacy-preserving verification practical across many domains without creating a new brittle trust island.
102.naive: A smart beginner would pick one familiar identity anchor and extend it. For mobile devices, keep using SIM credentials. For web services, keep using IP addresses, accounts, certificates, or platform login. For Web 3.0 applications, keep using wallets and ledger records. Then add encryption around the channel and publish a few smart contracts for auditability. That fails because each anchor leaks or concentrates trust in a different way. SIM records and account databases can be breached. IP addresses are weak identity signals. Wallets and ledger history can reveal behavior. Encryption protects messages in transit, but it does not prove that a hidden computation followed a rule. It also does not answer whether today's cryptography can survive tomorrow's quantum-capable attackers.
102.ap: The workshop's core move is to bring several boundary-control tools into one deployment conversation. Zero-knowledge proofs are the verification tool: they let one party prove that a hidden fact satisfies a public rule without showing the hidden fact itself. Blockchain infrastructure is the shared-record tool: it gives many parties a common place to check proofs, identity events, protocol actions, or audit trails without relying on a single operator. Post-quantum migration is the time-horizon tool: it asks which identities, wallets, ledgers, and protocols must be rebuilt before future attacks make older mathematical locks unsafe. The workshop also narrows the discussion to practical outputs. It emphasizes real deployments, empirical measurement, interoperability across Web and non-Web domains, a practitioner adoption playbook, a standards checklist, reproducible benchmarks and datasets, and a catalog of failure modes with mitigations. That makes the contribution a coordination mechanism for building trustworthy infrastructure, not a single algorithm.
102.mech: The mechanism is a workshop pipeline rather than a method pipeline for one experiment. The input is a collection of deployment problems from domains named in the abstract: finance, mobility, healthcare, AIoT, public services, supply chain, and AI or machine learning. Each problem contains a boundary: a user, device, service, or organization has something private, but another party needs evidence that a rule was followed. The workshop then sorts those cases by the trust function they need. Some cases need identity beyond SIM, IP, or NFT style anchors. Some need Layer-2 proving and verification, where many proof-related operations are moved off the main ledger path so the base chain is not overloaded. Some need ZKML, where claims about machine-learning computation are checked without exposing private model inputs or internals. Some need TEE plus ZK integration, meaning a protected hardware execution area is combined with a proof so outsiders can verify what was computed. Some need post-quantum migration for identities, wallets, ledgers, and protocols. Across these cases, participants compare what must be proven, what must stay hidden, where the proof is recorded, what standards are needed for other systems to read it, and what costs or failures appear in practice. The outputs are not predictions or labels; they are adoption guidance, interoperability checks, reproducible measurement artifacts, and a failure-mode catalog.
102.math: The central mathematical idea is proof under limited disclosure. In ordinary life, proving a claim often means showing the evidence. Zero-knowledge proof systems separate those acts. A prover holds private material, such as an identity secret, device credential, computation trace, or wallet-related fact. A public rule says what must be true: this device is authorized, this computation followed the agreed procedure, this ledger action is valid, or this protocol step satisfies its constraints. The proof convinces a verifier that the rule passed while revealing no more than that pass result. The second idea is a shared append-only record. A blockchain links records so many parties can check the same history and notice attempted rewriting. That fits decentralized infrastructure because trust comes from many checkers following the same rules, not from one database owner. The third idea is future-resistant hardness. Post-quantum cryptography uses mathematical problems believed to remain hard even for quantum computers, because old locks may become easy later. The tradeoff is verification versus cost, privacy versus inspectability, and long-term safety versus migration pain. The workshop matters mathematically because these tools are individually narrow, but Web 4.0 systems need them composed into usable identity, compute, and interoperability patterns.
102.dots: This paper belongs in the privacy, federated, and security family because it asks what useful signal may cross a boundary while private material stays hidden. It connects directly to USIM-less authentication work in the repo: both question whether mobile identity should keep depending on SIM-centered records. It also sits beside ZK-V for autonomous-driving simulation and Blind-QEM for quantum error mitigation, because all three use the same deeper move: prove that a rule was followed without exposing telemetry, circuits, credentials, or proprietary computation. The post-quantum thread connects it to the quantum-safe blockchain tutorial, where the problem is not only present-day privacy but the lifetime of signatures, wallets, and ledgers under future attacks. The blockchain thread connects it to trust and provenance work: a shared record helps only if the cryptographic claims inside it remain checkable and interoperable. ZABAPAD is therefore a connective workshop across privacy, security, networked identity, verifiable compute, standards, and systems measurement.
102.ww: The workshop approach works, if it works, because the problem is larger than any one proof system. A zero-knowledge proof can show that a particular statement is true without opening the private object, but it does not by itself decide which statement a regulator, vehicle, wallet, hospital, or edge service should ask for. A blockchain can preserve a shared audit trail, but it does not by itself make the proof fast, cheap, or understandable across domains. Post-quantum cryptography can replace vulnerable locks, but migration fails if identities, wallets, ledgers, and protocols are upgraded separately with incompatible assumptions. ZABAPAD's practical structure addresses that coordination gap. Benchmarks turn vague performance claims into comparable measurements. Interoperability checklists force builders to name the formats, protocols, and trust assumptions that must match. Failure-mode catalogs preserve negative evidence, such as where proofs are too costly, where hardware trust is misplaced, where standards do not line up, or where a privacy guarantee covers only the narrow checked statement. That shared map should reduce repeated mistakes.
102.po: The payoff is practical guidance for a difficult infrastructure transition. The abstract promises four concrete outputs: an adoption playbook, an interoperability and standards checklist, reproducible benchmarks and datasets, and a catalog of failure modes and mitigations. Those outputs would help builders decide when zero-knowledge proofs, Layer-2 proving, protected execution, blockchain records, and post-quantum upgrades are appropriate. The value is especially clear for finance, mobility, healthcare, AIoT, public services, supply chain, and AI or machine-learning systems, where trust failures can mean privacy exposure, forged identity, unverifiable computation, or systems that cannot communicate across organizational boundaries.
102.limits: The abstract describes a workshop agenda, so it does not prove that any particular zero-knowledge system, blockchain design, protected-execution setup, or post-quantum scheme is best. It assumes Web 4.0 and AIoT systems will need decentralized, privacy-preserving, verifiable connectivity, but it does not give deployment evidence for a specific architecture. It also does not specify benchmark definitions, datasets, cost targets, threat models, or standards bodies. Zero-knowledge proofs verify only the rule that was encoded; they do not prove surrounding software, incentives, hardware, or governance are sound. Blockchain records can preserve bad or incomplete claims as easily as good ones. The promised impact depends on practitioner participation and adoption.

103.bp: Internet standards are not just rule books. They are agreements about how real machines should talk to one another when the network is large, old, unevenly implemented, and full of competing needs. An RFC may say what a protocol requires, but the reason for a requirement often lives elsewhere: in working group email, long debate, rejected alternatives, compatibility worries, cost concerns, and compromises between clean design and deployable design. This paper serves learners and implementers who need more than the final command. If a developer reads an ambiguous specification without knowing why a choice was made, they may implement the letter of the rule while missing the operational intent. The paper treats standards rationale as buried evidence. Its goal is to retrieve the discussions that explain a design decision, then generate a clear account of the motivations and constraints behind that decision.
103.wh: The hard part is that the useful explanation is separated from the formal rule. RFCs are polished documents, while the design logic may be scattered across years of IETF working group messages and deliberations. Those messages are informal, numerous, redundant, and unevenly explicit. Some emails may contain decisive rationale; many others may contain procedural talk, partial proposals, objections, or context that matters only when placed beside another message. A simple standards reader sees the final text, but not the path that produced it. A simple search system sees matching words, but not whether a message actually explains a motivation, records a tradeoff, or names a constraint. A generation system then faces a second difficulty: if it receives too much archive text, it costs more to process and may blur the key rationale; if it receives too little, it may produce a smooth explanation without enough support.
103.naive: A smart beginner would search the RFC text and the mailing list for the same protocol terms, collect the top matching emails, and ask a language model to summarize them. That is sensible because the rationale should often mention the same feature, option, or requirement as the final standard. It fails because word overlap is a weak proxy for design logic. An email can mention a rule while merely quoting it, objecting to a side issue, or discussing deployment logistics. The truly important message may use different wording, because people debate motivations before final terms stabilize. The beginner might also paste a large chunk of archive history into the model, but that raises processing cost and gives irrelevant context the chance to crowd out the decisive explanation.
103.ap: The paper's central move is to build a retrieval-augmented generation system specialized for standards rationale. Retrieval-augmented generation means the answer model is not asked to explain from memory alone; it is first given outside evidence selected from a document collection. Here, the collection is not ordinary web pages but IETF email archives and working group deliberations. The retriever is tailored to find context rich in rationale, not just context that repeats protocol vocabulary. After retrieval, the generator turns the selected evidence into clear explanations of why protocol design decisions were made, including motivations and constraints. The important concrete shift is from rules-only reading to evidence-backed rationale reconstruction. The system tries to make buried deliberation available to people who were not present in the working group, while keeping the returned context much shorter than broad archive dumps.
103.mech: The input is a standards question or design decision whose surface form appears in an RFC, plus a large archive of informal IETF discussion around the relevant working group. The system first has to search that archive. Instead of treating every email that shares protocol words as equally useful, the tailored retriever looks for messages likely to carry rationale: explanations of why an option was accepted or rejected, statements of practical constraints, mentions of tradeoffs, or deliberation around a design choice. It returns a compact set of evidence rather than a sprawling history. That compactness matters because the next stage, the generation model, can only use what is placed in front of it and incurs cost as the context grows. The retrieved messages are then transformed from conversational fragments into an explanatory answer. The answer should connect the final standard rule to the reasons and constraints found in the archive. What comes out is not a new standard and not a general protocol tutorial, but a rationale explanation: why this design decision may have made sense given debate, compatibility, implementation, and practical compromise. The abstract reports two coupled outputs from the mechanism: better targeted email discovery at larger search scales, and shorter contexts for the generation stage.
103.math: The main mathematical idea is evidence selection under uncertainty. The archive is a large pile of possible witnesses, and each email may or may not help explain the design decision. Retrieval turns that uncertainty into a ranking problem: candidate messages receive scores so the system can decide which few should be read first by the generator. Ranking is not claiming that an email has one true value; it is a practical ordering for scarce attention. Similarity is part of the search because the system must measure closeness between the current standards issue and archived discussion, but the needed closeness is rationale closeness, not just word closeness. Matching also appears: a design decision must be paired with the small set of deliberation fragments that actually fit it. Information is the deeper currency. A useful email is one that rules out possible explanations by saying what constraint, concern, or rejected alternative shaped the rule. The tradeoff is completeness versus cost. More messages may contain more evidence, but they also add noise and processing expense. A tailored retriever is valuable if its scores preserve the rationale-bearing messages while compressing away repeated or irrelevant discussion.
103.dots: This paper sits in the repo's retrieval-augmented generation family because it changes where trust is earned in a generated answer: the explanation should be grounded in retrieved archive evidence, not fluent guesswork. It also belongs to the information-retrieval-search family, where the shared object is a huge collection and the task is to surface the few pieces that actually help. Its closest neighboring ideas are ranking, similarity, matching, and information. Ranking orders emails for use; similarity decides which discussions are near the design decision; matching pairs a rule with the deliberation that explains it; information asks which messages reduce uncertainty about why the rule exists. Compared with conflict-aware or pruning-oriented retrieval papers in the repo context, this work is less about adversarial evidence or multi-hop question trees and more about historical rationale extraction. It shares the same pressure: outside evidence is necessary, but unmanaged evidence can be too long, too noisy, or too costly.
103.ww: The mechanism should improve over the naive approach because standards rationale has repeated surface signs that ordinary keyword search does not fully use. Messages that explain decisions often contain reasons, constraints, objections, alternatives, or compromise language. A retriever tuned for rationale-rich context can learn to prefer those messages over emails that merely repeat a protocol term. That changes the generator's job. Instead of receiving a broad heap of archive text and having to infer what matters, it receives a smaller working set that is more likely to contain the actual design logic. Shorter context also helps for a plain reason: every extra irrelevant message competes for attention and cost. If the selected context contains the strongest witnesses, the generated explanation can be clearer and more faithful to the archived debate. The improvement is not magic from the language model alone; it comes from changing the evidence placed before the model. The system works when retrieval removes clutter without removing the fragments that explain the decision.
103.po: The payoff is practical transparency for Internet standards. Learners can understand not only what an RFC says but why it was shaped that way. Implementers can interpret ambiguous specifications with less dependence on private knowledge held by protocol authors. The abstract also reports an operational gain: the tailored retriever improves targeted email discovery, especially when searching at larger scales, while returning much shorter contexts. That means the system is aiming for both better evidence and lower generation cost. The broader capability is turning informal working group memory into accessible explanations of protocol motivations and constraints.
103.limits: The claims depend on the archive containing enough explicit rationale to recover. If decisive reasoning happened off-list, in meetings not represented in the data, or through tacit expert knowledge, retrieval cannot find it. The system also assumes it can distinguish rationale-rich discussion from merely related discussion; wrong ranking could produce confident but incomplete explanations. Shorter context saves cost, but it can omit nuance or minority objections. The abstract does not prove that generated explanations are authoritative replacements for RFC text, working group consensus, or expert review. It shows a path toward making rationale more visible, not a guarantee that every design decision can be reconstructed faithfully.

104.bp: This paper is about an unusually practical kind of finance problem: deciding whether a blockchain trader can complete a profitable three-step trade before the opportunity disappears. In decentralized finance, people trade through automated market makers, which are software pools holding pairs of assets. Their prices can disagree across pools. If a trader can move through three pools in a cycle, ending with more value than they started with, the trader can capture arbitrage profit. The word atomic matters because the whole sequence is executed inside one blockchain transaction: either all three swaps happen together or none do. That removes some uncertainty about partial execution, but it does not make the decision easy. The trader must choose the ordered three-pool route and the trade amount while facing wallet balance, pool liquidity, gas cost, and blockchain delay. The paper serves the real system where a slow perfect answer can be less useful than a fast good one.
104.wh: The hard part is that profit is not attached to a path alone or an amount alone. A path that looks profitable for a tiny trade may become bad when the trade is larger because the pool price moves as the trade consumes liquidity. A large trade may earn more before fees, but it can also hit wallet limits, drain a pool too much, or lose its edge after gas costs. The order of the three pools matters because each swap changes the asset held before the next swap. Blockchain latency adds another pressure: other searchers are hunting the same patterns, and prices can change before a slow calculation is usable. The abstract says exhaustive grid search gets the highest returns, which means careful enumeration can find strong choices. But it also says that search takes too much inference time for on-chain execution. The central tension is therefore not just finding profit. It is finding profit quickly enough to act.
104.naive: A smart beginner would list every possible triangular route, try many trade sizes on each route, subtract gas, reject anything that violates wallet balance or pool liquidity, and choose the largest remaining profit. That is the exhaustive grid-search idea in plain terms: cover the decision table with many candidate points and inspect them. It is attractive because it respects the concrete structure of the problem and can find the best answer among the candidates it checks. It fails operationally because the table is too slow to scan when the answer is needed within milliseconds. In blockchain arbitrage, a theoretically better route is worthless if another searcher acts first or if the pool state changes while the search is still running.
104.ap: The paper's core move is to turn the arbitrage choice into a learned action policy. A policy is a rule that looks at the current situation and immediately chooses what to do. Here the situation includes the available pools, the trader's balance, the liquidity constraints, gas costs, and the possible three-pool sequences. The action is not merely "trade" or "do not trade". It jointly chooses an ordered path of three pools and a trade amount. The score is net profit after the real constraints are considered. The authors formulate this as a constrained optimization problem, meaning the system searches for the choice that gives the best score while staying inside hard boundaries such as balance and liquidity. Because that search space is non-convex, with bumps and traps rather than one smooth bowl, they train a reinforcement-learning agent using Proximal Policy Optimization, a method that updates the policy cautiously from feedback so it improves without changing too wildly at once.
104.mech: The mechanism starts with a snapshot of the DeFi trading setting. The inputs are the candidate automated-market-maker pools, the possible ordered three-pool cycles, the wallet balance available to the searcher, the liquidity inside the pools, the gas cost of submitting the transaction, and the time pressure created by blockchain latency. For each possible action, the system must know two things: which three pools are used and how much value is sent through the first swap. That amount then flows through the first pool, becomes a new asset amount, flows through the second pool, and finally through the third pool back toward the starting asset. The raw gain is the difference between the final amount and the starting amount. The net gain subtracts gas and rejects or penalizes choices that exceed wallet balance or pool liquidity. Exhaustive grid search would repeatedly simulate this for many routes and many amounts. The proposed agent instead learns a shortcut from experience. During training, it tries actions in simulated or historical market states, receives a reward based on profit under the constraints, and adjusts its policy toward actions that tend to work. Proximal Policy Optimization keeps each update near the previous policy, so learning is incremental rather than reckless. Once trained, the agent no longer scans the whole grid. It maps the current state to a path and amount in milliseconds, producing a profitable candidate quickly enough to be practical.
104.math: The main mathematical object is a constrained choice problem. There is a set of possible routes, a range of possible trade sizes, and a score attached to each pair: net profit after fees and constraints. The constraints are not decoration. Wallet balance says the trade cannot spend more than the searcher has. Pool liquidity says the trade cannot assume unlimited depth. Gas cost says a grossly profitable trade may become unprofitable once the chain fee is paid. Latency says computation time itself has economic cost. The abstract calls the problem non-convex. In everyday terms, the profit surface is uneven: moving the trade size slightly can help in one region and hurt in another, and there may be several local peaks rather than one obvious best point. Reinforcement learning enters because the system can learn a policy from repeated action and reward. The policy is a reusable decision rule. Proximal Policy Optimization is a cautious update rule: after seeing which actions earned profit, it changes the policy, but limits the size of each change so the learned behavior does not swing from one extreme to another. The key tradeoff is speed versus profit. Grid search spends time to inspect many choices. The learned policy compresses past search experience into a fast decision rule, accepting that it may miss the absolute best point.
104.dots: This paper connects to several recurring conference ideas through one shared pressure: choosing under constraints when the choice space is too large for hand rules. It sits naturally in the optimization concept group because it defines what counts as good, net profit, and searches over controllable choices, path and amount, while respecting costs and limits. It also belongs to the reinforcement-learning family because the useful behavior is learned from action and feedback rather than written as a fixed rule. The DeFi angle links it to other repo records about blockchain markets, including ranking-dependent DeFi participation and stochastic CEX-DEX arbitrage. Those papers use different tools, but they share a practical fact: decentralized systems are open, fast, and rule-bound, yet their incentives create advantages for actors who can reason about timing, liquidity, rank, or price movement. The paper also brushes against systems thinking because inference latency is a first-class result. In this setting, computation time is not just engineering overhead; it changes whether the financial decision can be executed.
104.ww: The learned approach works when the market states seen during training contain repeated structure. Automated market-maker pools are not arbitrary boxes: their prices respond systematically to trade size and liquidity, gas costs enter as a predictable subtraction, and wallet limits cut off impossible actions. A policy can therefore learn patterns such as which path shapes tend to remain profitable after fees, when a larger trade causes too much price movement, and when a smaller but faster choice is enough. The advantage over the naive grid is that the policy carries memory of many previous searches in its learned parameters. At execution time it does not need to rediscover the whole profit surface from scratch. Proximal Policy Optimization helps because it learns through feedback while avoiding huge policy jumps that could destroy previously useful behavior. The abstract's result matches the intuition: exhaustive search still gets higher returns, because it checks more possibilities, but the trained agent reaches consistent positive profit with millisecond-level inference. In this market, being nearly right quickly can beat being exactly right too late.
104.po: The payoff is a practical arbitrage engine for a time-sensitive DeFi setting. The paper does not claim that the learned agent beats exhaustive search in raw profit. It claims something more operational: exhaustive grid search finds the highest returns but is too slow for on-chain use, while the PPO agent produces consistent positive profit with millisecond-level inference latency. That buys a deployable speed-profit compromise. It also makes the tradeoff explicit for MEV extraction: the best solver is not simply the one with the highest simulated return, but the one whose answer arrives before the blockchain opportunity is gone.
104.limits: The claim depends on the training and evaluation states resembling the market states faced during deployment. If liquidity patterns, gas costs, latency, or competing searcher behavior change sharply, the learned policy may choose paths that used to work but no longer do. The abstract does not prove that PPO always respects every operational risk outside the formulated constraints, nor that consistent positive profit survives all chains, tokens, fee regimes, or adversarial competition. It also reports that exhaustive grid search earns more, so the method knowingly trades some profit for speed. The result is strongest when millisecond inference is essential and approximate profitable choices are acceptable.
